notes: Chislev is a month in late autumn. The king is not named until 2:1; the narrative dates events by his reign.
The cupbearer served the king’s drinks and held a position of access and trust. The closing sentence explains how Nehemiah can approach the king.
vocabulary: Covenant
A binding relationship with commitments. Nehemiah appeals to God’s covenant faithfulness while confessing Israel’s failure.
Fear your name
Reverence for God, expressed here as a desire to honor him.

notes: Nisan falls in spring. Both this scene and 1:1 are dated to the twentieth year; the text does not explain its year-reckoning.
The queen’s presence is stated, but her identity and role in the decision are not explained.
Nehemiah receives a military escort. Ezra 8:22 describes a different decision about an escort; the accounts are not made identical.
Tobiah’s title is literally “servant.” It can describe an official; it does not by itself establish that he was enslaved.
The three terms deny the opponents a share, a recognized claim, and a memorial in Jerusalem. The precise legal force of the final term is uncertain.
vocabulary: Susa
A royal center of the Persian Empire, far east of Jerusalem.
The good hand of my God
An image for God’s favorable help, recurring in Ezra and Nehemiah.

notes: The Hebrew says the nobles would not bring their necks into the work of “their masters.” The reference may be to supervisors or to their Lord.
“Old Gate” may instead be the proper name “Jeshanah Gate.”
The phrase involving the governor’s throne can indicate his jurisdiction or a location associated with his seat of authority.
The verb rendered “restored” is difficult here; “left untouched” is another proposed sense.
Shallum’s daughters are explicitly included among those doing the repairs.
This Nehemiah, son of Azbuk, is distinct from the narrator, Nehemiah son of Hacaliah.
Zaccai follows the Hebrew reading tradition recorded beside the written form Zabbai.
“Upper” may describe the royal house or the projecting tower; the compact wording leaves the attachment uncertain.
vocabulary: Consecrated
Set apart for sacred use. The priests consecrate the gate and their section.
Muster Gate
A gate name associated with inspection or appointment; its exact location is uncertain.

notes: Public 4:1–6 corresponds to Hebrew 3:33–38; public 4:7–23 corresponds to Hebrew 4:1–17. The source records are preserved without omission.
The question about restoring the wall is difficult. Proposals include leaving the builders to themselves or allowing them to restore it.
The prayer asks for retaliation and for the opponents’ guilt not to be erased. Its force is retained as part of the narrated conflict.
The warning’s Hebrew wording is difficult. It can be understood as a repeated appeal for the workers to return home, or as a warning that enemies would attack from every direction.
The final words are exceptionally compressed: literally, “each his weapon, the water.” Keeping weapons while going for water is one possible reading; the exact action is uncertain.
vocabulary: Burden bearers
Workers who carried building materials and cleared debris.
Our God will fight for us
Nehemiah’s assurance to the workers; it is part of his speech in the threatened city.

sections.1: Debt and the enslavement of families

notes: The families describe their sons and daughters being enslaved for debt, with some daughters already enslaved. Their complaint is not softened to ordinary employment.
The vocabulary can refer to lending, debt claims, or interest. The “hundredth” in verse 11 is one percent of the listed goods, but the text gives no time interval for the charge.
The verse states forty shekels of silver in addition to food and wine; it does not specify a daily interval for this amount.
vocabulary: Shekel
A unit of weight used for silver payments.
The governor’s food allowance
Provision claimed by a governor from the governed population. Nehemiah says he declined it.

notes: “The villages” may instead be the place-name Kephirim.
Gashmu is the form used here for Geshem, named in 2:19 and 6:1.
“Now strengthen my hands!” turns abruptly from reporting threats to an appeal. God is not named in this short clause.
Shemaiah’s confinement is unexplained. Nehemiah’s question about entering the temple and living may involve ritual danger as well as the proposed escape from attackers.
Noadiah is explicitly identified as a female prophet. Nehemiah’s prayer includes her among those who tried to frighten him.
vocabulary: Elul
A late-summer month. The wall is completed on its twenty-fifth day, after fifty-two days of work.
Bound by oath
Committed through a sworn obligation; these ties complicate Nehemiah’s opposition to Tobiah.

notes: The reading tradition has “I said,” which keeps Nehemiah as the speaker. The instruction to delay opening until the sun is hot is unusual and is retained.
This register parallels Ezra 2 but differs in several names and counts. Each list is translated as it stands; the figures are not harmonized.
Nephishesim follows the reading tradition; the corresponding name in Ezra 2:50 is Nephusim.

The pinned Hebrew source has no horse-and-mule verse corresponding to the usual 7:68. This edition therefore proceeds from v67 to v69, as the existing verse labels do. Its public 7:69–73 binds Hebrew 7:68–72. No line is imported from Ezra 2:66.
The Hebrew gives “thirty and five hundred” priestly robes, rendered 530. The wording is not altered to create a separate silver contribution.
vocabulary: Urim and Thummim
Sacred means of priestly decision. The disputed priestly families must wait for an authorized decision.
Daric
A monetary unit used for the gold gifts. Ancient coin identifications and weights are not fully certain.

sections.1: The instruction is read and explained
sections.9: A holy day for shared joy

notes: The reading is made clear and its meaning given so the people understand. The wording may include interpretation or translation, but it does not name a second language.
“The joy of the LORD” may mean joy found in the LORD or joy associated with him. “Stronghold” retains the protective image.
The identification of the “oil tree” is uncertain; wild olive and other resinous or oily trees have been proposed. It is listed separately from the olive tree.
The Hebrew uses the name Jeshua for Joshua son of Nun. “Like this” qualifies the claim about the celebration; the verse need not mean that no observance at all had occurred since Joshua.
vocabulary: Instruction
Hebrew torah: teaching or instruction, including the written law of Moses.
Festival of Shelters
The festival also called Booths or Tabernacles, marked by living in temporary shelters.

notes: Bani occurs twice in the list as written. The names have not been silently consolidated.
“Sea of Reeds” renders the Hebrew name traditionally called the Red Sea. The name alone does not settle the crossing’s location.
“In their rebellion” follows the pinned Hebrew. Some readings instead have “in Egypt”; that change is not adopted here.
The prayer’s quotation has the singular “This is your God,” although Exodus 32:4 uses a plural formulation. The wording here is preserved.
The wording about the allotted territories is compressed and uncertain. The two named Amorite kingdoms remain distinct.
This verse is Hebrew 10:1. The word for the written commitment is not the usual Hebrew word for covenant, though the undertaking has a solemn communal character.
vocabulary: Faithful love
Enduring, committed kindness. The prayer repeatedly contrasts God’s mercy with the people’s rebellion.
Slaves
The speakers describe foreign rule over their land, produce, bodies, and livestock as servitude.

notes: Public 10:1–39 corresponds to Hebrew 10:2–40; the preceding Hebrew verse appears as public 9:38.
Nebai follows the recorded reading tradition beside the written form Nobai.
The annual contribution is one-third of a shekel here. It is not changed to the half-shekel amount found in other passages.
Bringing firstborn sons under the instruction does not mean sacrificing them. The law distinguishes redemption of human firstborn from animal offerings (Exodus 13:13; Numbers 18:15–16).
vocabulary: A curse and an oath
A sworn commitment that invokes a penalty for breaking it.
Tithe of the tithe
The Levites give a tenth of the tithes they receive to support the priests.

notes: “Shilonite” is the form given here. Its relationship to the family of Shelah or to Shiloh is debated.
The phrase rendered as second in charge can instead refer to the city’s Second Quarter.
The final expression can mean a prominent family or be read as the personal name Haggedolim.
Jeduthun follows the Hebrew reading tradition.
Being “at the king’s hand” describes Pethahiah’s service as a royal representative in the people’s affairs.
vocabulary: Casting lots
A method used here to select one in ten people to live in Jerusalem.
Daily provision
An assigned support for the singers’ work.

notes: Jonathan here and Johanan in verse 22 are retained as distinct written forms; the genealogy is not silently harmonized.
Melichu follows the reading tradition beside the written form Malluchi.
No family head is supplied after Miniamin in the Hebrew. The incomplete pair is left visible rather than assigning Piltai to both families.
The Hebrew reads “Jeshua son of Kadmiel.” It is not changed to “Jeshua and Kadmiel” to match another list.
The compact list can be grouped in different ways; some interpreters distinguish singers among its first three names from the following gatekeepers.
The second procession goes the other way around the wall. The wording does not require an exact modern compass direction.
vocabulary: Dedication
Setting the rebuilt wall apart with celebration, thanksgiving, and purification.
Thanksgiving choirs
Groups whose songs of thanks accompany the two processions along the wall.

sections.4: Restoring the temple rooms and support

notes: The term describes a mixed population; its precise membership is not specified. It should not be reduced to a claim about mixed biological ancestry.
Eliashib’s closeness to Tobiah may indicate kinship or an association; the wording does not identify the exact relationship.
Artaxerxes is called “king of Babylon” here, although he is the Persian ruler. The title is retained.
The children’s speech is described in relation to Ashdod and Judah and to the languages of other peoples. The concern about language is stated in the narrator’s account.
Nehemiah reports cursing, beating, and pulling out hair. These coercive actions are retained plainly, without endorsement or euphemism.
vocabulary: Abandon the house of God
The complaint recalls the promise in 10:39 and focuses here on neglected support for temple workers.
Remember me
Nehemiah’s recurring appeal closes the book; the narrative does not announce that every conflict has been resolved.
